newsitem.title: MEXICO: Dying Indian takes Zapatista message across Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Dying Indian takes Zapatista message across Mexico.

text.p: A dying rebel Indian woman set out on Thursday from her dirt-poor village in southern Mexico toward the bustling capital -- a journey that casts her as an unlikely symbol of the Zapatista rebellion against Mexico's government.

Stricken with cancer, the diminutive Tzotzil woman was the surprise solution to 11th-hour talks between the government and rebels over their plans to attend an Indian congress in Mexico City despite government warrants for their arrest.

Government officials had also warned that a Zapatista trip to the seat of government power would signal the end of peace talks that have dragged on-and-off since the rebels launched their January 1994 uprising.

"She is the most belligerent, aggressive and intransigent member of the Zapatista Army for National Liberation," charismatic rebel leader Subcommander Marcos told reporters and supporters in this remote village on Wednesday in announcing that the woman would represent the rebels at the conference.

"Before dying, she wished to speak with other Indians," he said. Wearing a trademark rebel ski-mask to hide her identity, Ramona -- her nom-de-guerre -- left in a car early on Thursday, escorted past makeshift army barracks by prominent Mexican leftists and some members of Congress.

Her trip marks the first leg of a two-day journey that will take her to a modern city of 18 million that is unlike anything most of her villagers have ever seen. She will represent her fellow rebels at the conference, spreading the guerrillas' gospel of Indian autonomy to representatives of the country's eight million indigenous peoples.
Mexican newspapers on Thursday said she could also seek medical treatment in Mexico City.

The elderly, infirm woman provided the Zapatistas with a fitting symbol of their initial uprising, which featured impoverished Indians armed sometimes only with old rifles and machetes squaring off against Mexican army tanks and planes.
The symbol of Ramona as a modern-day David battling Goliath was not lost on Mexico's press, which called her choice as the Zapatista envoy a shrewd public relations move.

Ramona was to travel from the colonial city of San Cristobal to Mexico City on a chartered plane on Friday in time for the conference's final day on the anniversary of Colombus' arrival in the New World, which is marked here with little celebration by Indians.

Her exit from the jungle marked the Zapatistas' symbolic break of a military stranglehold that was placed on them after their uprising. Thousands of troops have created makeshift barracks on the outskirts of the jungle in recent years, creating pressure on the Zapatistas to lay down their arms.
